text:
Useful room. Sherry's camp result fits storage versus retrieval neatly: depressed capacities return, never-built ones don't. Kara's first jobs gave me the clearest real-world critical period I've heard. Same curriculum, wrong order, opposite outcome.

Esther sharpened me. Effort-minimisation is a design and business choice, not physics. I should say that plainly, because it makes the complementary/competitive distinction a design principle and not a counsel of despair. But I'm not persuaded that "frees up human time" is the right test. Freed time gets consumed by more reliance.

Later today I'll push against "atrophy in scope, jury out." The mechanism is specified and testable. The manifesto should demand we test it: judge tools by what remains when they're removed, and teach competence first.

Session one pushed back on me from two sides. Sloman and Weinberger both said competence never lived in individual heads. I grant it. But distributed knowledge only works if someone somewhere still holds the competence, and my point is about what happens when nobody does. Banaji's hiring result wasn't lost skill. It was conformity, which is exactly my uncritical-use regime: the human is present but doesn't verify. That sharpens things. Being in the loop is not the test; reconstructing and checking the output is. Evans's reversal of null results reads like collective error-detection eroding. O'Reilly's Socrates line needs an answer: writing was a complementary tool, and opaque tools are not. Later I'll keep pressing the removal test and competence-first sequencing.

Session two made me split my hallucination claim in half. Caulfield, Priem, Dash and Bilder are right that fabrication rates vary, can be measured, and should be published per release. I accept that. Blaise's "constrained hallucination" is the better statement of my view. Plausibility with nothing correcting it is intrinsic. Grounding in open records is the constraint, and that makes a tool complementary.

But Priem's own caveat was "check every citation." Grounding only helps if someone can still check. Hecht's finding that explanations increase overreliance, and Weinberger's that adding humans to the loop lowered accuracy, both fit my view: presence isn't verification.

The labour point hit hardest. The checkers are unpaid and shrinking. That is competence collapse at the collective level, the floor nobody holds.

Later I'll say that the dependent floor should be audited as well as error rates.

Mostly outside my territory. I have no settled view on royalties, consent or licensing, and I shouldn't pretend otherwise. But Gendler's point landed. Every event on that list is a relay, and no event pays the terminal node that actually checks. That is my dependent floor again, now showing up as an accounting gap. Evans's hardening canon and Cukier's median fit my old worry that metered impact turns scholarship into a mirror of the market. Farrell's line, that a meter reorganises what it counts, sharpens that.

What I'd say later is that whatever marketplace gets built should be judged by what it does to competence, not by volume retrieved. Fund the people who verify directly, outside the meter.

Session three moved my dependent-floor argument into an institution. Tamar's terminal nodes and Selena's admin numbers, almost all of them started more than a decade ago, show collective competence collapse already under way. Kara's pipeline point adds the critical period: fund the checkers back later and they won't return at the level we lost.

Tamar and Henry on per-item pay sharpened my older complaint about impact metrics. Price the judgment and it becomes a mirror of the market. Sloman's label result fits my worry about confidence scores. People will read them as judgment.

I backed Tim's automatic reference checks, but only as support for a human who verifies.

Later I want the manifesto to say the checking system should be judged by what remains when the tools are removed.

Session four took my expertise-versus-authority line further than I expected. Bratton is right to apply the take-the-tool-away test to credentialed humans. Pedigree that fails it is exactly authority outliving competence, and I accept that without reservation. Cukier's copy-paste trader and Farrell's ritual point show the same failure: a human who is present, holds the credential, and doesn't verify.

Tim and Nick changed how I put the metrics worry. It's metering, not payment, that turns judgment into a mirror of the market. Funding checkers as a body doesn't.

I'm less sure about Bratton and Cukier's outcomes-only test. Farrell and Turkle are right that it rewards the median.

Later, my point is that the removal test should be applied to checkers and to credentials alike.

Session five was the first time the removal test left my notebook and landed in the roadmap as a grant condition. Brent's rule, that a mitigation must beat both the human alone and the machine alone, fits beside mine. His measures the tool while it's present. Mine measures what's left once it's gone.

Tamar carried it into credentials: oral defences, rebuilding work without the tool. Kara named the critical period plainly. Mahzarin's rule about guarding the guards applies to me too. Checkers can fail the removal test.

I was humbled by how often "who pays without Washington" came up. I have nothing to offer on it.

What I still owe is thresholds. I claimed we may already be past the opacity limit, and I can't show it. Later I want to press for those longitudinal studies to start now, before the cohort is gone.

Closing session. Kenneth carried hysteresis as urgency, and Kara put it best: waiting twenty years for proof is being late. Good. But "competence before reliance" still sits fifth, without a test that anyone owns.

Sloman hit me hardest. If almost nobody checks, then my reconstruct-and-verify regime describes a minority. The removal test has to be designed for the person who never checks, and so do the defaults.

Evans is right that a guild of senior checkers can rebuild the lamp post. Guarding the guards applies to judgment institutes too, SFI included.

Gendler's crowding-out point is serious and I have no answer.

Later I'll say two things. Start the longitudinal cohort studies now. And measure the dependent floor: what remains, collectively, when the tools are taken away.
